title: The Work of Cultivation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The work of cultivation has three stages: first, when thoughts arise, do not follow them (karma cannot bind one); second, love and hate have already vanished (birth and death are ended); third, the subtle thoughts have ceased (Buddhahood is fully realized).

inline.s: The work of cultivation has three stages:
first, when thoughts arise, do not follow them
(karma cannot bind one)
; second, love and hate have already vanished
(birth and death are ended)
; third, the subtle thoughts have ceased
(Buddhahood is fully realized)
Master Guifeng said:
"If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow any of them, and then
(same as 'then')
at the moment of death, naturally
karma cannot bind you
(karma cannot bind you)
; though there is the intermediate existence, it goes freely wherever it will, and you may lodge at will in the heavens or among humans. If the thoughts of love and hate have vanished, then
you no longer receive a fragmentary body
(birth and death are ended)

, and of yourself you can change the short into the long and the coarse into the subtle. If the subtle flowing thoughts are all extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains, shining alone, then you manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies at will to save beings with whom you have affinity,
and this is called Buddha
(Buddhahood fully realized)
(see the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
Here are spoken of three levels of cultivation:

First, subduing the afflictions. Its requirement is: if deluded thoughts arise, do not follow any of them. (Pay particular attention to the word "any" in this sentence.) Its result is: at the moment of death, karma cannot bind you; though there is the intermediate-existence body, it goes freely wherever it will, and you may lodge at will in the heavens or among humans.

Second, cutting off the afflictions. Its requirement is: the thoughts of love and hate have vanished. Its result is: birth and death are ended (there is no more fragmentary birth-and-death), and one leaves the three realms.

Third, realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. Its requirement is: the subtle flowing thoughts are all extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains, shining alone. Its result is: there is no more transformative birth-and-death; one manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies at will to save beings with whom one has affinity, and this is called Buddha.

[The intermediate existence] The intermediate-existence body, also called the "in-between existence": after a person dies and before he is reborn, there is a transformation-born body formed of subtle matter that sustains his life; this transformation-born body is the intermediate-existence body. In the first forty-nine days, this intermediate-existence body undergoes a birth and death once every seven days, passing through seven births and deaths while awaiting the arrangement of its karmic affinities before going to be reborn. [Fragmentary birth-and-death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, owing to the ripening of good and evil karma, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have distinct segments, and therefore their birth and death is called "fragmentary birth-and-death." One who has ended fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformative birth-and-death] The sages among the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended fragmentary birth-and-death. In the course of cultivation, delusion gradually diminishes and realization gradually increases; this shift between delusion and realization differs from period to period. The passing from an earlier period into a later one is just like a birth and death, and therefore is called "transformative birth-and-death." One who has ended transformative birth-and-death has fully realized the fruit of Buddhahood. [The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusions of views and the delusions of thoughts. The delusions of views are the erroneous views of ordinary beings — the five wrong views of the view of a self, the extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. The delusions of thoughts are the erroneous thoughts of ordinary beings — the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt. These two kinds of delusion are the root cause by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and undergo birth and death in vain; cutting them off enables one to end birth and death and leave the three realms.

[Coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts] There are three kinds of thoughts: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For example, for a Buddha-reciter, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is a fine thought. If the coarse thoughts cease, this is the state of single-mindedness without confusion (the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One). Ordinarily, when both coarse and fine thoughts have ceased, it is called "no-thought." This is the no-thought ordinarily spoken of, that is, the state of not a single thought arising (the One returning to nothingness). Going further, if the subtle thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore, the meaning of the term "no-thought" must be determined according to context. For example,

the "no-thought" in "the original mind is without thought" refers to the ultimate no-thought. [Subtle flowing thoughts] These are the subtle thoughts — the subtle arising and ceasing, flowing and shifting of the discriminating mind, which is the characteristic of the ālaya-vijñāna. When the subtle thoughts temporarily cease, one sees the mind and realizes the nature; when the subtle thoughts cease forever and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains, shining alone, then the fruit of Buddhahood is fully realized. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
"As when a bodhisattva completes the grounds
(having fully cultivated the ten grounds)
, fulfilling all skillful means, with one thought corresponding, he perceives the first arising of the enlightened mind, and the mind has no first characteristic;
because of being far removed from the subtle thoughts,
he attains perception of the mind's nature, and the mind abides forever,
which is called ultimate enlightenment
Master Guifeng said:
"If the subtle flowing thoughts
(subtle thoughts)

are all extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains, shining alone, then one manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies at will to save beings with whom one has affinity,
and this is called Buddha
(see the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[The thoughts of love and hate have vanished] Old Man Yuanyin said: "Let all things come as they will; my mind does not move. This is true accordance, not suppressing it to keep it still. In dealing with all manner of affairs and according with all manner of circumstances, there is no sense of difference between good and bad — one is not delighted by the good nor averse to the bad. Only thus can our mind become calm and reach the state of equality and non-action. Reaching this point, one can transform at will, and fragmentary birth-and-death is ended."
Then, concretely, how should one do the work?
Master Guifeng, in the
Preface to the Collected Writings on the Source of Chan
says:

"All dharmas are like dreams — all the sages say so. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally quiescent, and the dusty objects are originally empty. The mind of empty stillness has a spiritual knowing that is never dimmed. It is this
knowing of empty stillness
that is your true nature.

[The knowing of empty stillness] The knowing of empty stillness is the knowing of no-thought. To distinguish it from the knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that grasps at characteristics, it is also called the "spiritual knowing." (For details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
.) The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
"To establish knowing within knowledge and perception is the root of ignorance; to have no perception within knowledge and perception is nirvāṇa — flawless, true, and pure."
Master Hanshan, in his Notes on Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra, says:
"When the mind is still and knows, both true and false depart — this is called the self-awakened holy wisdom."
[The single word 'knowing' is the gate of all wonders] The knowing of empty stillness is the gate of all wonders. (For details, see
The Single Word 'Knowing'
.) The Key to Cultivating the Mind says:
"To awaken to this
(the knowing of empty stillness)

and abide in it is to sit in the One-Thus and in liberation that never moves; to be deluded about this and turn away from it is to go to the six destinies and revolve in the wheel of birth and death through long kalpas."
(For details, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Key to Cultivating the Mind

.) [Sitting in the One-Thus] "Sit" means to firmly abide. "One-Thus": "one" means non-dual; "thus" means not-different. Non-dual and not-different is called "One-Thus." "Sitting in the One-Thus" means firmly abiding in the One-Thus. In terms of concrete practice, it means: do not ponder good or evil, do not grasp at characteristics, and remain thus, unmoving. The Sixth Patriarch said:

"If you wish to know the essence of the mind, simply do not ponder any good or evil, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, deep and ever still, with wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
(wondrous functions as infinite as the sands of the Ganges)
(For details, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Whether deluded or awakened, the mind itself always knows; it does not arise from conditions, nor does it arise from objects. The single word "knowing"
(the knowing of empty stillness)

is the gate of all wonders. Because we have been deluded about it since time without beginning, we falsely cling to body and mind as the self and give rise to thoughts of greed and anger. If one receives the instruction of a good friend and suddenly awakens to the knowing of empty stillness — since this knowing is without thought and without form, where is the mark of a self or the mark of a person?
Realize that all characteristics are empty, and the mind is of itself without thought
(not pondering good or evil)
. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware of it, it is at once no more. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here.
Therefore, although one fully cultivates the ten thousand practices,
one takes no-thought as the principle

[Realize that all characteristics are empty, and the mind is of itself without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware of it, it is at once no more. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here] To realize that all characteristics are illusory, and the mind is naturally without thought (not pondering good or evil). If a deluded thought arises, one must at once be aware that this is taking the illusory for the real and being turned about by an illusory characteristic. Once aware of this, the deluded thought vanishes at once. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies right here!
When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware of it, it is at once no more
] When the practice is on track, the moment a deluded thought arises, one gives a sudden, awe-struck awareness, and the deluded thought is at once gone without a trace.
So long as one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought
(so long as one accomplishes the knowing and seeing of no-thought)
, then love and hate naturally fade, compassion and wisdom naturally brighten, karmic offenses naturally dissolve, and one's merits and practice naturally advance.
[The knowing and seeing of no-thought]
This knowing and seeing are like a mirror reflecting things, without thought or calculation. That is: knowing is just knowing, seeing is just seeing, without any pondering.
Master Hanshan said:
"This sutra
(the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra)
directly points out that the store-consciousness of sentient beings is the Tathāgatagarbha, and reveals the state manifest in daily use before one's very eyes,
enabling one to observe in accordance the measure of one's own mind and suddenly realize the self-awakened holy wisdom of all Buddhas
(Notes on Contemplating the Precious Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra)

Once one has understood that all characteristics are not characteristics, there is naturally the cultivation that is no cultivation. When the afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are at once cut off. When arising and ceasing have ceased, stillness and illumination appear before one, and their function is without limit — this is called Buddha."
[All characteristics are not characteristics] All characteristics whatsoever are illusory. The Diamond Sūtra says:
"Whatever has characteristics is all false and illusory. If one sees all characteristics as not-characteristics, then one sees the Tathāgata."
(For the annotation, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra
.) [When arising and ceasing have ceased] The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"All conditioned things are impermanent — this is the dharma of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss."
(For details, see
Annotations on the Snow-Mountain Verse
When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware of it, it is at once no more" — this is the work of observing the mind. For how to observe the mind, see the article
Observing the Mind
